summary.text: The Aufbau principle says that in an atom's or ion's ground state, electrons first fill the lowest-energy subshells and then move on to higher-energy ones.
Filling this way gives the most stable electron configuration possible, so the 1s subshell fills before the 2s.
Subshells fill in order of increasing n + ℓ, and when that sum ties, the subshell with the lower n goes first.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: German for 'building-up principle', not a scientist's name

facts.label: Rule-breaking elements
facts.value: Twenty elements differ from the Madelung prediction

items.prompt: An atom is building up past argon. Subshell A has n = 4 and ℓ = 0, while subshell B has n = 3 and ℓ = 2. Which fills first, and why?

options.label: A, because its n + ℓ sum is lower
B, because its n value is lower
Neither, since both fill at the same moment
B, because it can hold more electrons

items.explain: A has n + ℓ = 4 and B has n + ℓ = 5, and subshells with a lower n + ℓ value are filled first.

items.prompt: Two subshells end up with exactly the same n + ℓ value. How is the tie settled?

options.label: The one with the higher n fills first
They share electrons equally between them
The one with the lower n fills first
The one with the higher ℓ fills first

items.explain: Where n + ℓ values are equal, the subshell with the lower n value is filled first.

items.prompt: Three orbitals of equal energy are open and three electrons arrive in them. How do the electrons settle?

options.label: Two share one orbital and the third takes another
Each takes its own orbital, all with the same spin
Each takes its own orbital, with spins alternating
All three crowd into the lowest of the orbitals

items.explain: Hund's rule says electrons occupy different orbitals of the same energy singly, with the same spin, before any are occupied doubly.

items.prompt: Copper's measured configuration differs from what the n + ℓ ordering predicts for it. Why does the real atom take that other arrangement?

options.label: The ordering rule only applies to atoms in an excited state
A copper atom always has one fewer electron than expected
Experiments in the lab disturb the electrons while measuring
Filling its d subshell puts the atom in a lower energy state

items.explain: By filling the 3d subshell, copper can be in a lower energy state, so the measured form is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than the predicted [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s².

items.prompt: Many laws carry a scientist's name. Why doesn't the Aufbau principle?

options.label: It is named after a German phrase for 'building-up principle'
It was a group effort, so nobody's name was chosen
Its discoverer asked for the rule to stay nameless
It was named for the place where it was first tested

items.explain: The name comes from the German Aufbauprinzip, meaning 'building-up principle', rather than from a scientist.

items.prompt: A student worries that copper and uranium break the filling order, so chemistry predictions must fail. What is the fair reply?

options.label: Those atoms are ignored because they are too rare to study
The energy gaps are tiny, and a nearby atom can change the preferred form
The periodic table was redrawn to match each exception
The exceptions only appear in atoms that carry a positive charge

items.explain: These exceptions are not very relevant for chemistry because the energy differences are small and nearby atoms can change the preferred configuration, so the periodic table ignores them.
